runs.analysis:
Stage fit: the stage asks for concise, strategically important assumptions, each one short sentence of 17 words or fewer, keeping the key numbers.

Candidate A: 30 single-idea bullets, most within or close to the 17-word limit. It keeps the key figures: €40B, 10-15% contingency, 20-30% weather reduction, 8,000-12,000 workforce, €3-8B trust fund, 70% hedging, 10 atm, 30-minute response, €500M-€2B insurance, 2-3 year baseline studies, and the 5/10/15% escalation triggers. Each bullet is one atomic assumption, so downstream stages can use it directly. It covers governance, phasing, technical, environmental, financial, social, safety and legal topics. The 30-item count is on the high side for "distill", but the bullets are tight.

Candidate B: 15 bullets, but many are long compound sentences well over 17 words (the surveillance, safety framework, stakeholder engagement and financing bullets). This breaks the length constraint and defeats the purpose of condensing. It bundles several assumptions into one bullet (contingency, operational reserve and hedging in one; emergency vessels, evacuation and insurance in another). Its first bullet only restates the plan prompt. It does add some useful details: contingency worked out as €4-6B, treaty ratification, the tranche-financing sources, and the IMO route. However, it drops items A keeps (escalation triggers, artificial reefs) and adds "veto rights" and "IMO" details whose source is unclear.

Overall: A follows the format and length constraints much better, keeps the numbers, and is more usable downstream. B is more verbose and less compliant.

The stage asks for short assumptions of at most 17 words each, with key numbers kept. Candidate A has 15 bullets, but many are far too long. The timeline, budget, governance, financing, treaty, and safety bullets each run about 25–35 words and pack several assumptions together. That breaks the "concise, one short sentence" rule and defeats the point of distilling. A's content is accurate and covers a lot, including treaty ratification, IMO assessment, and tranche financing. Candidate B has 30 bullets, almost all single-idea sentences of about 10–17 words, and they keep the key numbers: 10–15% contingency, 20–30% weather reduction, 8,000–12,000 workforce, €3–8B trust, 70% hedging, 12-month reserve, €500M–€2B insurance, and 30-minute response. B is somewhat redundant: phasing appears in two bullets, and the weather-window and monitoring points repeat. Some items are minor, such as the 5/10/15% escalation triggers and artificial reefs, and 30 bullets is a lot for a "distilled" list. B still follows the format constraint much better, and its atomic assumptions are easier for downstream stages to use. It also drops A's treaty ratification and financing-source detail, but it keeps the ICC arbitration, bilateral framework, and tranche-funding-cliff points. Overall, B fits the stage better.

Candidate A covers the plan's key strategic assumptions in 25 short bullets, nearly all within the 17-word limit: the 9 GW target and timeline, phase timeline, the €100B–€140B budget, building heights and hall sizes, PUE and cooling, the split-campus model, the anchor-tenant gate, fiber, the security review, and the treatment of external approvals as uncertain. Downstream stages would find these useful. A's flaws are minor: it repeats the RTE non-binding consultation point, the 80% buffer and 25% biodiversity bullets are not reconciled, "Phase 1 limited to 500 MW" narrows the prompt's 500 MW–1 GW range, and the 2 GW heat load and 75% apprentice figures may be upstream inventions. Candidate B has only 8 bullets that read like a truncated version of A's first items. They are accurate in places, but they omit most strategic basics (9 GW, timeline, budget, tenant gate, security review, fiber, heat reuse, uncertainty of external approvals), and several exceed the 17-word limit. B is incomplete as a distillation. A's breadth and key-number retention outweigh its minor redundancy and inconsistency.

Stage: condense assumptions into concise, strategically important ones (short sentences, ≤17 words, keep key numbers). Candidate A has 8 bullets, mostly concise, but it omits many central plan facts (budget, phasing, split-campus, uncontrolled external approvals, tenant gates) and contains some questionable items (it asserts a "€4.32B unhedged" figure without the hedge basis). Candidate B is longer (24 bullets), which is less "condensed", but it carries the key numbers and constraints from the prompt: budget, phases, power, PUE, height, hall counts, tenant gate, fiber, and the treatment of external approvals as uncertain. That makes it much more useful downstream. B also has some internal inconsistencies: it says 80% is a buffer and also 25% is a biodiversity/community allocation, which are roughly compatible but redundant; the 75% apprentice requirement seems invented; the 2 GW district heating target is dubious; the "14–30 m" height and "subsea contingent on Phase 3+" are mildly invented; and the ">17 words" limit is probably satisfied by most bullets. B clarifies the FX assumption ("only 70% hedged"), which makes the €4.32B figure interpretable. Overall B is more faithful to the plan's skeptical posture (no binding commitments, non-binding RTE consultation) and more complete. A is tighter, but too thin and omits key things. B has some redundancy and invented details, but it is still better overall.

Both candidates distill assumptions from an upstream document we can't see, so I judge them on faithfulness to the plan prompt, concision, and usefulness.

Candidate A covers the plan's key facts: the €1.5B budget, the 18/30/60-month timeline, the four corridors, the 40% target, and the scope. It also keeps the upstream assumption details: the €200M float, the T+3 settlement, the 5% fee cap, the 60%/10% budget split, 35 FTEs, the 65% consensus rule and the liability rules. It has some errors and inconsistencies:
- It says "Paris-Amsterdam" for the first corridor, dropping Brussels and Köln.
- It says accessibility and reduction cards are deferred "12 months beyond core ticketing (month 30 mandate)", which is muddled.
- "Provisional binding at 6 months, final at 18 months post-launch" conflicts with the plan's "binding standards within 18 months" of start.
- Some bullets run past 17 words.
- The "Builder scenario" label and "Secondary transport modes deferred" are plausible but may not come from the upstream document.
Overall it is broad and useful for downstream stages, since it restates the plan's core numbers and scenario.

Candidate B stays mostly within the upstream-style assumptions, with short sentences. It has several problems:
- It is heavily redundant: provisional binding at six months appears in three bullets, the liability rule in three, and the royalty cap in two.
- It leaves out the plan's central facts: the budget total (only as a percentage), the corridors, the 40% target, the timeline, and the mode integration.
- It includes an "aggressive enforcement posture" with a "three strikes" rule, which conflicts with the "realistic, not aggressive" scenario instruction.
- "EU backstop limits compensation to connecting failures between the first and last known segment failures" is garbled.
- Some details are useful: the 90-minute backstop threshold, the 99% T+3 figure, and the correct euro conversions (€900M and €150M).

A is more complete and more useful for downstream stages, though it has some inconsistencies. B has more redundancy and less coverage of the plan. A is better overall.

Both candidates distill assumptions but we lack the upstream assumptions file, so judge on faithfulness to the plan and internal consistency.

A: It has many redundant or duplicate items. API fee caps appear twice. Provisional binding at six months appears three times. Binding standards at 18 months and the tiered liability/100% compensation are each stated twice. It contradicts itself on the backstop: "delayed/missed exceeding 90 minutes" versus "between first and last known segment failures". It adds an "aggressive enforcement posture" with 'three strikes', which conflicts with the "realistic, not aggressive" instruction. Its "30-month grace period" is unclear. Several lines are vague, such as the "T+5 minutes" benchmark at month 6. It omits the key plan anchors: the 40% target, the 30-month API mandate, the five-year horizon, and the corridors. Some lines run over 17 words. Overall it is redundant and lacks coverage.

B: It is more diverse and anchors on plan facts: the €1.5B budget, the 18/30/60-month timeline, the 40% target, the corridors, 20+ operators, and OSDM. It states the realistic scenario. It has some flaws. "Paris-Amsterdam" and "Madrid-Barcelona" shorten the corridors. "Deferred 12 months beyond core ticketing (month 30 mandate)" is slightly odd. The deferral of bus/ferry/air integration may conflict with the plan's "integration hooks", but it is a plausible assumption. A few lines run over 17 words. It is less redundant, and the 35 FTE breakdown is specific. It is better for downstream use.

B is clearly better.

Candidate A gives about 28 assumptions that cover most of the plan's pillars: the budget split and the €1.5M Month 4 release, the three-level alert system and thresholds, governance and alert authority, cooling center tiers and accessibility, transport, outreach and field safety, GDPR and aggregate data, home interventions and procurement lead time, analog communications, the Month 4 gate metrics, primary outcomes and the Year-2 plan. Most bullets are short and keep the key numbers. A has some flaws: the "Monthly 4 gate" typo, a mild inconsistency between "direct subsidy vouchers" and "procured locally with 4-week lead time", and some redundancy between the two-person teams and geotagged dispatch bullets. Its Level 2 threshold (day >30°C, night >19°C) is logically coherent for hot nights. Candidate B has only 8 bullets. It omits the gates, transport, multilingual and analog communications, worker protection, metrics, the no-construction assumption, the Year-2 and cost model assumptions, and the top-floor and social housing targeting. It also has errors: "Night < 19°C" is wrong for a heat alert, and "mid-March (T+6 weeks)" conflicts with a 3 May 2026 start. B is concise but too thin for downstream stages and contains a substantive error. A is clearly better on completeness, correctness and usefulness.

Candidate A is concise (8 items) but has a logic error: it sets the Level 2 night threshold as "Night < 19°C", which is backwards for hot-night alerts. It also gives a "mid-March (T+6 weeks)" readiness target even though the project starts in May, so the date is inconsistent. It omits many key assumptions: the three-level alert system, the Month 4 gate metrics, no construction, the GDPR limits, low smartphone use, the transport target, the home-intervention approach and the city. Candidate B states the threshold correctly (day >30°C with night >19°C). It captures nearly all key numbers and constraints: the budget split, the 12 FTE plus 10 two-person teams, the gate metrics, 14-hour staffing, the CRM cost, the Leipzig calibration and the analog channels. Its items are mostly within 17 words. Weaknesses are that 30 items is less condensed, a few items overlap, and "Monthly 4 gate metrics" is awkward. Overall B is more faithful, consistent and useful downstream.
